locations/muslim-quarter/timeline.description: Jerusalem came under Muslim rule; the sacred precinct and the city's institutions developed through successive Umayyad, Abbasid and Fatimid periods.
After Salah al-Din recaptured Jerusalem in 1187, religious and charitable institutions were renewed around the Haram and its approaches.
Sultans and governors endowed madrasas, ribats, fountains, markets and residential buildings along the western and northern approaches to Al-Aqsa.
The governor Tankiz al-Nasiri completed Souq al-Qattanin, its monumental gate and associated commercial and bath complex.
Religious and commercial institutions continued under Ottoman administration, and the quarter remained a centre of Old City life.
Homes, schools, worship routes and family businesses continue amid conservation, access and economic pressures.

locations/muslim-quarter/quiz.question: Which Mamluk market forms a monumental approach toward Al-Aqsa?
locations/muslim-quarter/quiz.explanation: Souq al-Qattanin is a vaulted Mamluk market whose eastern gate opens toward the Haram al-Sharif/Al-Aqsa compound.
locations/muslim-quarter/quiz.sourceNote: Muslim Quarter §4–5; Museum With No Frontiers, Suq al-Qattanin

locations/muslim-quarter/quiz.question: Under which governor was Souq al-Qattanin completed in 1336–1337?
locations/muslim-quarter/quiz.explanation: The market and associated complex were completed under the Mamluk governor Tankiz al-Nasiri in 737 AH/1336–1337 CE.
locations/muslim-quarter/quiz.sourceNote: Muslim Quarter §2 and §5; Museum With No Frontiers

locations/muslim-quarter/quiz.question: Which architectural detail should visitors look for at the Qattanin entrance?
options: Alternating stone colours and inscription bands
locations/muslim-quarter/quiz.explanation: The monumental entrance uses coloured stonework, carving and inscription bands typical of prestigious Mamluk portals.
locations/muslim-quarter/quiz.sourceNote: Muslim Quarter §5 and §9; Jerusalem Studies, Khan Tankaz

locations/muslim-quarter/quiz.question: Why is the Muslim Quarter described as more than an archaeological district?
options: It is a lived neighbourhood of homes, schools, worship and trade
locations/muslim-quarter/quiz.explanation: Its heritage includes continuing residential, educational, religious and commercial life, not monuments alone.

locations/muslim-quarter/quiz.question: Which Christian devotional route crosses part of the quarter?
locations/muslim-quarter/quiz.explanation: The Via Dolorosa passes through the quarter, adding a Christian pilgrimage route to its overlapping urban histories.

locations/christian-quarter/timeline.description: Constantine's Church of the Holy Sepulchre was dedicated around the place central to the church's sacred traditions.
The Fatimid caliph al-Hakim ordered major destruction of the church.
A Byzantine-sponsored restoration reopened the sanctuary, although not in its original complete form.
Crusader rebuilding unified key holy places beneath a Romanesque church, dedicated on 15 July 1149.
A destructive fire was followed by substantial restoration, especially around the rotunda and the structure over the tomb.
Shared use by several churches became governed by the Status Quo; pilgrimage and local commerce continued around the sanctuary.

locations/christian-quarter/quiz.question: Which arrangement regulates shared responsibilities at the Church of the Holy Sepulchre?
locations/christian-quarter/quiz.explanation: Several Christian communities share spaces and responsibilities under the historic Status Quo arrangements.

locations/christian-quarter/quiz.question: In which year was Constantine's Holy Sepulchre complex dedicated?
locations/christian-quarter/quiz.explanation: The Constantinian church was dedicated in 335 CE over a site identified in Christian tradition with Calvary and the tomb.
locations/christian-quarter/quiz.sourceNote: Christian Quarter §2; Oxford Reference, Church of the Holy Sepulchre

locations/christian-quarter/quiz.question: What major architectural phase was dedicated in 1149?
options: The Crusader rebuilding of the Holy Sepulchre
locations/christian-quarter/quiz.explanation: Crusader builders unified major sacred spaces into much of the Romanesque church form visible today.
locations/christian-quarter/quiz.sourceNote: Christian Quarter §2; JSAH Crusader reconstruction study

locations/christian-quarter/quiz.question: What should visitors notice on the church's entrance façade?
locations/christian-quarter/quiz.explanation: The entrance has paired Crusader-period Romanesque portals; one remains sealed while the other is used.

locations/christian-quarter/quiz.question: Why can circulation inside the church change without notice?
options: Active services and processions share the building
Visitors must follow a fixed museum tour
locations/christian-quarter/quiz.explanation: It is a living, shared place of worship, so ceremonies and processions may temporarily alter visitor movement.

locations/armenian-quarter/timeline.description: Armenian pilgrimage and religious presence in Jerusalem became established after Armenia's adoption of Christianity.
Much of the present Cathedral of St James took shape during the Crusader period while preserving earlier traditions and material.
The Armenian Patriarchate established a printing press in Jerusalem, an important centre of Armenian-language publishing.
A large pilgrim guesthouse was built; the complex later served other community purposes and now houses the Armenian Museum.
Armenian ceramic artists arriving in Jerusalem helped create the city's distinctive school of hand-painted tile and pottery.
The Edward and Helen Mardigian Museum reopened after major renewal, presenting Armenian Jerusalem and survivor histories.

locations/armenian-quarter/quiz.question: Which craft became a distinctive Armenian contribution to modern Jerusalem?
locations/armenian-quarter/quiz.explanation: Armenian artists arriving from 1919 developed a distinctive Jerusalem school of painted tile and pottery.
locations/armenian-quarter/quiz.sourceNote: Armenian Quarter §2 and §5; Tel Aviv University ceramics history

locations/armenian-quarter/quiz.question: When did the Armenian Patriarchate establish its Jerusalem printing press?
locations/armenian-quarter/quiz.explanation: The printing press was founded in 1833 and became an important centre of Armenian-language publishing.
locations/armenian-quarter/quiz.sourceNote: Armenian Quarter §2 and §5; St James Printing House research

locations/armenian-quarter/quiz.question: Much of the present Cathedral of St James dates to which period?
locations/armenian-quarter/quiz.explanation: Much of the current cathedral took shape during the twelfth century while preserving earlier traditions and fabric.

locations/armenian-quarter/quiz.question: What was the nineteenth-century building now used by the Armenian Museum originally built for?
locations/armenian-quarter/quiz.explanation: It was built in the 1850s as a pilgrim guesthouse and later served community and refugee needs before becoming a museum.
locations/armenian-quarter/quiz.sourceNote: Armenian Quarter §2; Associated Press museum report

locations/armenian-quarter/quiz.question: Which detail best helps identify the Armenian Quarter in the street?
options: Blue-and-white ceramic plaques and Armenian script
locations/armenian-quarter/quiz.explanation: Armenian inscriptions, carved cross-stones and hand-painted ceramic plaques mark the community landscape.

locations/maghariba-quarter/timeline.description: Salah al-Din restored Muslim rule in Jerusalem after the Crusader period.
Historical accounts associate an Ayyubid charitable endowment with housing Maghrebi pilgrims and residents near the sanctuary.
Homes, religious institutions and endowed properties formed a compact community beside Bab al-Maghariba and al-Buraq Wall.
Photographs and surveys documented the quarter's dense stone fabric and North African institutions.
Most of the quarter was demolished and its residents displaced; sources commonly document roughly 135 structures removed.
The open plaza differs radically from the former neighbourhood; family memory and archival evidence preserve its history.

locations/maghariba-quarter/quiz.explanation: Historical accounts associate the charitable endowment with 1193 CE, soon after Salah al-Din restored Muslim rule.

locations/maghariba-quarter/quiz.question: What happened to most of the quarter on 10–11 June 1967?
options: It was demolished and residents were displaced

locations/maghariba-quarter/quiz.explanation: Most of the built fabric was demolished and residents were displaced, leaving a radically changed urban setting.

locations/maghariba-quarter/quiz.explanation: Archival images, records and attributed family testimony help reconstruct the erased lanes and social fabric.

locations/sheikh-jarrah/timeline.description: The neighbourhood name became associated with a tomb traditionally attributed to Hussam al-Din al-Jarrahi, a physician linked in tradition to Salah al-Din.
Prominent Jerusalem families built stone residences north of the Old City as urban life expanded beyond the walls.
The Isaf al-Nashashibi house was built to a design attributed to architect Spiro Khouri, combining local stone architecture with modern villa planning.
Villas, consulates, hospitals and institutions reinforced the district's modern urban character.
Twenty-eight refugee families entered a housing arrangement involving Jordanian authorities and UNRWA; 28 housing units were completed in 1956.
Community life continues amid prolonged legal, property and displacement pressures that require current verification.

locations/sheikh-jarrah/quiz.question: When did prominent Jerusalem families expand housing in Sheikh Jarrah outside the walls?
locations/sheikh-jarrah/quiz.explanation: Prominent Palestinian families built residences there during Jerusalem's late nineteenth-century expansion.

locations/sheikh-jarrah/quiz.question: When was the Isaf al-Nashashibi house completed?
locations/sheikh-jarrah/quiz.explanation: The house was completed in 1922 and its design is attributed to architect Spiro Khouri.

locations/sheikh-jarrah/quiz.question: How many housing units do UN records note as completed in 1956?
locations/sheikh-jarrah/quiz.explanation: UN documentation records completion of 28 units connected with an arrangement for 28 refugee families.
locations/sheikh-jarrah/quiz.sourceNote: Sheikh Jarrah §2 and §5; United Nations records

locations/silwan/timeline.description: The spring and valley supported settlement beside Jerusalem's historic core; water channels and rock-cut systems belong to several phases.
Medieval geographer al-Muqaddasi described the spring and the cultivated landscape below Jerusalem.
Silwan was an established village whose residents cultivated irrigated gardens and hillside terraces.
Photographs documented the village's dense stone houses and terraced relationship to the Kidron Valley.
Population and building expanded across the slopes while farming and spring memories remained part of local identity.
Archaeology, tourism, homes and community life occupy the same contested landscape and must not be conflated.

locations/silwan/quiz.question: Which medieval geographer described the spring and cultivated landscape below Jerusalem?
locations/silwan/quiz.explanation: The tenth-century geographer al-Muqaddasi described Jerusalem's water and cultivated landscape.

locations/silwan/quiz.explanation: Homes, paths and terraces respond to a steep valley-side landscape that is best read vertically.

options: Only one of them is real
They are different evidence layers sharing the same landscape
locations/silwan/quiz.explanation: Ancient remains and contemporary Palestinian life overlap spatially but answer different historical and social questions.

locations/at-tur/timeline.description: The ridge served as an eastern approach to Jerusalem and a place of burial, worship and cultivation.
Christian pilgrimage buildings were established on the Mount of Olives and near Gethsemane in the Byzantine period.
Churches and pilgrimage routes were rebuilt or reorganised around sites identified in Christian tradition.
The Palestinian village community and multiple religious institutions continued across the ridge.
The present Basilica of the Agony/Church of All Nations at Gethsemane was consecrated; Antonio Barluzzi designed it above earlier remains.
At-Tur developed into a dense Jerusalem neighbourhood while retaining major sacred sites, cemeteries and panoramic viewpoints.

locations/bab-al-amud/media.subject: Bab al-Amud market activity in 1920
locations/bab-al-amud/media.arabicSubject: الحركة التجارية عند باب العامود سنة 1920
locations/bab-al-amud/media.description: A 1920 Matson Collection photograph shows wheat-laden camels being unloaded outside Bab al-Amud, documenting the gate plaza as a regional arrival and trading space.
locations/bab-al-amud/media.arabicDescription: تظهر صورة من مجموعة ماتسون سنة 1920 تفريغ حمولة القمح من الجمال خارج باب العامود، موثقةً الساحة فضاءً للوصول والتجارة الإقليمية.

locations/bab-al-amud/media.description: A crisp wide view captures the Ottoman gate’s crenellations, flanking towers, pointed portal and the stepped civic plaza that gathers below it.

before.subject: Damascus Gate
before.arabicDescription: صورة أرشيفية من مجموعة ماتسون توثق باب العامود وساحته سنة 1925 قبل إعادة تشكيل المجال الحضري الحديث.

after.subject: Damascus Gate
after.arabicDescription: مشهد حديث لباب العامود سنة 2025 يتيح مقارنة الواجهة والساحة وحركة المشاة بالصورة التاريخية للموقع نفسه.

locations/bab-al-amud/timeline.description: A Roman gate complex was built during the reign of Hadrian as the city was refounded as Aelia Capitolina; remains survive below the present entrance, and the Arabic name is believed to recall the column in its plaza.
The Madaba mosaic map represented the northern gate, an internal plaza and a column marking the start of the main north-south street.
The present gate was built as part of the Ottoman walls commissioned by Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent.
Photographs documented the gate as a busy arrival point for people, animals and goods from northern routes.
Archaeological work exposed parts of the earlier Roman gate beneath the Ottoman structure.
The steps and square remain a major Palestinian civic gathering place and threshold to Old City markets.

locations/bab-al-amud/quiz.question: The visible monumental façade of Bab al-Amud belongs mainly to which period?
locations/bab-al-amud/quiz.explanation: The present façade was built in 1537–1540 as part of Sultan Suleiman's Ottoman walls, above earlier remains.

locations/bab-al-amud/quiz.question: What is the likely origin of the Arabic name Bab al-Amud, “Gate of the Column”?
options: A column shown in the Roman plaza
locations/bab-al-amud/quiz.explanation: The sixth-century Madaba map shows a column in the inner Roman plaza, remembered in the Arabic name.
locations/bab-al-amud/quiz.sourceNote: Bab al-Amud §2 and §3; University of Michigan gate record

locations/bab-al-amud/quiz.question: During whose reign was the earlier Roman gate complex built?
locations/bab-al-amud/quiz.explanation: The Roman gate complex dates to the reign of Hadrian, when the city was refounded as Aelia Capitolina.
locations/bab-al-amud/quiz.sourceNote: Bab al-Amud §2; University of Michigan gate record

locations/bab-al-amud/quiz.question: Why does the gate passage turn instead of running straight through?
options: To create a defensive bent entrance
To make room for a railway
locations/bab-al-amud/quiz.explanation: The bent-axis passage controls movement and prevents a direct approach through the fortification.

locations/bab-al-amud/quiz.question: Which market route continues south after entering the gate?
locations/bab-al-amud/quiz.explanation: Khan al-Zeit carries the route into the Old City through a roofed commercial street.

locations/bab-al-amud/related.name: Christian Quarter
locations/bab-al-amud/related.description: A quarter of churches, monasteries, hospices and markets centred on the Church of the Holy Sepulchre.

locations/bab-al-amud/related.name: Muslim Quarter
locations/bab-al-amud/related.description: The Old City’s largest quarter, shaped by Mamluk architecture, living markets and routes leading toward Al-Aqsa.

locations/bab-al-amud/related.name: Armenian Quarter
locations/bab-al-amud/related.description: A compact historic quarter known for St James Cathedral, Armenian institutions and Jerusalem’s ceramic tradition.
